The HIV and AIDS Pandemic. In the early 1980s, a global health crisis emerged. The first cases were identified in 1981 when clusters of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and Kaposi's sarcoma appeared in young gay men in Los Angeles. The virus causing AIDS, called HIV or human immunodeficiency virus, attacks the immune system. Since its emergence, it has killed an estimated 40 to 45 million people through 2024.

HIV is believed to have jumped from non-human primates to humans in Central Africa, likely through bushmeat hunting in the early to mid-twentieth century. The virus transmits through sexual contact, blood exposure, and mother-to-child transmission. It initially spread rapidly through sexual networks and unscreened blood transfusions. By the early 1990s, AIDS was the leading cause of death for Americans aged 25 to 44.

The turning point came in 1996 with antiretroviral therapy, particularly combination approaches. This development transformed HIV from a death sentence into a chronic manageable condition. Sub-Saharan Africa was and remains disproportionately affected. At the pandemic's peak, over 7 percent of the population in countries like South Africa and Botswana were HIV-positive.

Activists and affected communities, including groups like ACT UP and TAG, forced rapid drug development, transparency in clinical trials, and equity in treatment access. They fundamentally reshaped the relationship between patients and researchers. These communities demonstrated that novel pathogens could be confronted through organized action and persistence.
